interview_metadata.name: Laura Bost
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) - Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up in Modesto, California, in a working-class family that was pretty tied to agriculture and the rhythms of the Central Valley. My dad did equipment and field work around orchards and packing operations, and my mom worked in produce quality control and seasonal office support, so a lot of my childhood was hearing about harvest schedules, irrigation, heat, and whether a crop was going to be good that year. We were not fancy people, but we had routines: family dinners when shifts allowed, church on and off when I was little, cousins around during holidays, and a lot of reminders to take care of what you have. I was the kid who wanted to know why things worked. I liked rocks, mirrors, batteries, leaf patterns, and taking pictures of anything small enough that other people ignored it. In high school, first in Modesto and then Atwater High after we moved, science fair became my thing. I also joined art club, so I had this split identity where one afternoon I would be troubleshooting a small solar cell demonstration and the next I would be trying to paint foothills in watercolor. I did not go straight to a four-year college after high school. Money was part of it, and honestly anxiety was part of it too; I was afraid of taking on debt and failing. Instead I worked, took technical certification courses in lab instrumentation and safety, and found my way into materials testing and then renewable-energy research support. Now I live in Atwater and work as a physical scientist in a lab setting, mostly designing and running Raman and FTIR experiments, keeping careful notebooks, processing data in Python or MATLAB, and helping characterize photovoltaic materials. I have never been married and I do not have kids. My relationships are a small circle: my parents, a younger brother, a couple of close friends, coworkers I trust, and hiking and yoga people I see regularly. The big theme of my life is probably trying to build something stable without becoming closed off. I plan too much, I budget too carefully, and I can spiral when I feel behind, but I also make room for things that keep me human: watercolor, macro photography, farmers market cooking, Sierra foothill hikes, puzzles, Kings games on TV, and looking through my little telescope when the sky cooperates.

follow_ups.question: When you picture childhood in Modesto, what is one scene that comes back clearly?
follow_ups.response: Standing near an almond orchard after dinner with my dad pointing out how dry the soil was. I remember the smell of dust and irrigation water, and him explaining that weather was not abstract when your paycheck depended on it.

follow_ups.question: Who encouraged the science and art sides of you when you were young?
follow_ups.response: My high school science teacher, Mr. Cardenas, really pushed the science fair side. For art, it was Ms. Rivas in art club; she made me feel like painting landscapes was not just a hobby for quiet kids.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was after high school. I had decent grades and a science teacher who thought I should go to college right away, but my family did not have a cushion, and I was very aware of what debt could do. I also did not have the confidence then to picture myself in a university physics department. So I chose a more practical route: I worked locally, took lab safety and instrumentation certifications, and got into testing work. At first I worried I had chosen the smaller life. But that route taught me how real labs function, how to document properly, how instruments fail, and how careful work matters. Later, when I got exposure to renewable-energy materials, I realized I still wanted the deeper science. That is why I am now trying to build toward applied physics graduate training and a research associate path, even if my route looks nontraditional.

follow_ups.question: What were the specific options in front of you then?
follow_ups.response: A community college transfer plan, trying for a four-year school farther from home, or working and doing certifications. I chose work plus certifications because it felt financially safer.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone disagree with your choice?
follow_ups.response: Mr. Cardenas was disappointed but kind. My parents were relieved I was being practical, though my mom kept saying I should not give up on school forever.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious, but it was also shaped by fear. I sat with a notebook and compared costs, commute, wages, and certificate timelines. I chose the option that felt survivable.

follow_ups.question: What did that notebook list look like?
follow_ups.response: Columns for tuition, gas, hours I could work, application deadlines, and what the certificate might qualify me for. Very Laura, honestly.

follow_ups.question: Do you still make decisions that way?
follow_ups.response: Yes. I use spreadsheets now, but the habit is the same: I calm myself down by turning a scary choice into rows and dates.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A stronger college counseling system or a mentor who understood nontraditional science paths would have helped. I did not know what bridge programs, scholarships, or lab technician pipelines were available.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have changed things most?
follow_ups.response: Someone sitting with me and saying, here are three realistic routes into science, with costs and deadlines. I needed specifics, not encouragement alone.

follow_ups.question: Do you try to offer that to anyone now?
follow_ups.response: A little. When interns or high school students visit the lab, I tell them there is not only one correct path.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner right now, and I do not have children. My parents are still very important to me. They live close enough that I can drive over for Sunday dinner a couple times a month, and we text about practical things like weather, appointments, and whether somebody needs help moving furniture. My mom is the emotional check-in person, though she sometimes worries in a way that makes me worry more. My dad is quieter, but he shows up if there is a car issue or something with the apartment. I also have a younger brother, Evan, who is 22. We are close in a teasing way; he thinks I over-plan everything, and I think he under-plans everything. Extended family matters too, especially around holidays, but I am closest to my immediate family. I sometimes feel behind because I am not married and do not have kids, especially around cousins who started families early, but I also know my current life needs space for work, school preparation, and getting my anxiety managed.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually two Sundays a month, sometimes more if there is a birthday or if my dad needs help with paperwork online.

follow_ups.question: What does a typical family dinner look like?
follow_ups.response: Something simple like chicken, beans, salad, or whatever my mom made in a big batch. We talk about work, gas prices, weather, and my brother's latest plan.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: No spouse or children. My immediate family is my mom, dad, and younger brother Evan. We are close, but I keep some emotional boundaries because everyone worries loudly in my family.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk with Evan often?
follow_ups.response: A few times a week by text, usually jokes or him asking me to explain a bill or form.

follow_ups.question: Do you have grandparents still involved?
follow_ups.response: One grandmother is still alive on my mom's side, but she is more extended family than daily support.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are Maya and Elise. Maya works in environmental compliance, and we hike or get coffee maybe twice a month. Elise is more of my art friend; we go to the Fresno Art Museum or Studio Art Gallery and sometimes paint together at her kitchen table. I also have a small board-game group, usually four or five people, and we meet every month or so. I am not dating anyone seriously right now. I have gone on dates, but I tend to move slowly and I need someone who respects that I like quiet time.

follow_ups.question: Who do you call when something goes wrong?
follow_ups.response: Usually Maya first, because she is calm and practical. If it is family-related, I call my mom.

follow_ups.question: What games does your board-game group play?
follow_ups.response: Wingspan, Ticket to Ride, Azul, and sometimes logic puzzle games. I cook too much food and usually put too much turmeric in something.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Atwater, California, in a modest apartment area that is mostly working families, young people starting out, and some older residents who have been here forever. It is not glamorous, but it is practical. I can get to groceries, work, and Highway 99 without too much trouble, and Merced and Fresno are reachable when I want museums, better restaurants, or a bigger farmers market. There are almond orchards and open stretches not far away, so it still feels connected to the Valley landscape. My street gets quiet early on weeknights, except for dogs and the occasional loud truck.

follow_ups.question: What places nearby are part of your routine?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, a small yoga studio, the library sometimes, and the route I take for evening walks when it is not too hot.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A few by face and first name. I am friendly but not deeply involved; I will bring in a package if I see one sitting out.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe, especially during the day. At night I am more cautious, so I avoid walking alone late and I pay attention in the parking lot.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you cautious?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-ins in the complex and one time a neighbor had a package stolen. Nothing violent that I have personally experienced.

follow_ups.question: What do you do to feel safer?
follow_ups.response: I park near lights, keep my car empty, and text a friend if I am getting home late.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is affordability compared with bigger California cities and being near family and outdoor places. The downside is heat, limited cultural options in town, and feeling like you have to drive for almost everything.

follow_ups.question: What do you miss that Atwater does not have?
follow_ups.response: More galleries, more quiet cafes open late, and better public transportation.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you there?
follow_ups.response: Rent I can manage, family nearby, and a familiar Valley feeling that I still care about.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is just me in a one-bedroom apartment. I like living alone because my work can be mentally noisy, and I need quiet when I get home. My apartment has a small desk area for data work and journaling, a corner where I keep watercolor supplies, and a shelf that is too full of science fiction books. No one is staying with me temporarily.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite part of living alone?
follow_ups.response: Control over the quiet. I can cook, stretch, read, or just sit without negotiating anyone else's noise.

follow_ups.question: Do friends or family visit often?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a month. Board-game nights happen at my place sometimes because I cook.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: It is just me, and I am the only permanent household member.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short-term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, nobody.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, I have lived alone here consistently.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one stays overnight regularly. A friend might stay after a late board-game night once in a while, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How rare is rare?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once or twice a year.

follow_ups.question: Family ever stays over?
follow_ups.response: No, they live close enough to go home.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No. No one else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is one?
follow_ups.response: Yes, just one.

follow_ups.question: Any pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets. I like the idea, but my schedule and budget say no for now.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are structured around work. I usually wake up around 6:15, make coffee and oatmeal or toast, check the day's lab schedule, and leave by about 7:20. Work runs roughly 8 to 4:30, though experiment days can stretch later. Monday and Wednesday evenings are usually data processing, laundry, or meal prep. Tuesday I try to do yoga if I am not exhausted. Thursday is often a walk or a call with family. Friday night is quiet, usually cooking and a show or reading. Saturdays vary: yoga in the morning, farmers market when I can, hiking with the Fresno Outdoor Club maybe once or twice a month. Sundays are errands, meal planning, family dinner some weeks, and getting ready for Monday.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 10:30 on work nights, though if I am anxious I will read until closer to midnight.

follow_ups.question: What is your most protected routine?
follow_ups.response: Sunday meal planning. If I skip it, the whole week feels more expensive and chaotic.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I work one main job as a physical scientist in renewable-energy materials research. The work is lab-based: setting up spectroscopic measurements, running Raman and FTIR scans, preparing samples, checking calibration, documenting everything, and then processing results. My usual schedule is Monday through Friday, about 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. If an instrument booking runs late or a sample batch has to be finished, I may stay until 6. I do not have a second paid job, but I spend some evenings studying applied physics and computational methods because I want to move into a research associate role.

follow_ups.question: What does a good workday look like?
follow_ups.response: The instrument behaves, the baseline is clean, I label every file correctly, and the data tells us something instead of just creating more questions.

follow_ups.question: What does a stressful workday look like?
follow_ups.response: A calibration issue, a deadline for a report, and three people needing the same instrument slot.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a pretty detailed budget and calendar. I check bills every Sunday, update my savings categories, and plan groceries around what is seasonal or on sale. I also journal a few nights a week because it helps with anxiety. I call or visit my parents regularly, and I sometimes help them with online forms or health appointment portals. I try to keep one creative block each week for watercolor or photography, even if it is just an hour.

follow_ups.question: What do you track in your budget?
follow_ups.response: Rent, utilities, gas, groceries, savings, medical copays, art supplies, and a small travel fund.

follow_ups.question: What do you write about in your journal?
follow_ups.response: Mostly what I am worried about, what actually happened, and what I can do next. It is a reality check.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is that I added more formal study time in the evenings. I am trying to prepare for advanced applied physics coursework, so I block two nights a week for math, Python, or reading journal articles. I also started using my smartwatch more seriously to track steps and elevation because I noticed I was sitting too much on data days. Yoga has become more regular too, partly because my shoulders get tight from lab and computer work.

follow_ups.question: When did you start that study schedule?
follow_ups.response: About six months ago, after a performance review where my manager encouraged me to think bigger about research roles.

follow_ups.question: Has it helped?
follow_ups.response: Yes, but it also makes me tired. I have to protect rest or I get brittle and anxious.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children, so I do not have a school-year routine for kids. My weekday routine is centered on work, errands, study, and staying connected with family and friends.

follow_ups.question: Do children play a role in your life through family or mentoring?
follow_ups.response: A little through cousins' kids and lab outreach events. I like explaining simple experiments to high school students.

follow_ups.question: Do you imagine having children later?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, but it is not immediate. I would need more stability and a partner I really trusted.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited. I have been pulled over once for a brake light, and it was tense because being stopped is tense, but it stayed polite and I got a fix-it warning. I have called the non-emergency line once about a suspicious car near the apartment parking area after there had been break-ins. I do not have a personal history of major police involvement, but I pay attention to how different people's experiences can be very different from mine.

follow_ups.question: What do you remember about the traffic stop?
follow_ups.response: My hands were shaking even though I had not done anything serious. I kept thinking about where my registration was.

follow_ups.question: Did the non-emergency call help?
follow_ups.response: They said they would increase patrols. I do not know if it changed anything, but I felt better having reported it.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: In high school there were resource officers, and I remember some students feeling watched more than protected. That stuck with me more as I got older.

follow_ups.question: Were those students mostly from particular groups?
follow_ups.response: It seemed like Latino boys and kids already labeled as trouble got more attention. I did not have language for it then.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it at the time?
follow_ups.response: Not much. I noticed it but kept quiet, which I regret a little.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested. No immediate family member has been arrested either. I know one former classmate who had a DUI, but we are not close now.

follow_ups.question: Did that affect your social circle?
follow_ups.response: Not really. It was someone I heard about through old classmates.

follow_ups.question: Any court or legal issues in your household?
follow_ups.response: No, nothing like that.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and usually in midterms, but I have missed some local special elections. I vote by mail because it lets me sit with the ballot, look up candidates, and not feel rushed. Local water, air quality, schools, and energy issues matter to me, so I have been trying to pay more attention to county and state races. I would not call myself an activist, but I do think voting is part of being responsible.

follow_ups.question: How do you research a ballot?
follow_ups.response: I use the county voter guide, CalMatters, candidate websites, and sometimes local newspaper endorsements if I can access them.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss voting with family?
follow_ups.response: A little. My parents are more moderate and practical; we talk more about issues than party labels.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would describe myself as center-left, maybe a moderate Democrat or left-leaning independent depending on the issue. Climate and renewable energy are very important to me, partly because of my work and partly because I grew up around agriculture and know how heat, water, and air quality affect real families. I support public investment in science, clean energy, community colleges, and rural education. I also believe health care should be easier to access and less terrifying financially. On social issues, I am generally progressive: I support LGBTQ rights, reproductive rights, and treating immigrants with dignity. At the same time, I come from a family where people worry about taxes, gas prices, and whether regulations understand small farms and working people. So I try not to talk like policy is simple. I trust science as a method, but I do not automatically trust every institution to implement things fairly. I want government that is competent, transparent, and grounded in local realities.

follow_ups.question: What issue feels most personal to you?
follow_ups.response: Climate and water in the Central Valley. It is not abstract here; it shows up in heat, smoke, crop decisions, and people's lungs.

follow_ups.question: Where do you feel less aligned with progressive politics?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes messaging ignores rural or working-class anxiety. If people feel talked down to, they stop listening even when the policy goal is good.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more focused on implementation and local government. When I was younger, I thought having the right values was enough. Now I care a lot about whether a program actually reaches people in places like Atwater or Modesto. The pandemic, wildfire smoke, and housing costs also made me more aware that stability is fragile for working people. I am still center-left, but I am more practical and less impressed by slogans.

follow_ups.question: What changed your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: Watching people argue online while local families were dealing with rent, smoke, school disruption, and medical bills.

follow_ups.question: Has your work influenced your politics?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. Lab work makes me value evidence, but it also shows me how funding priorities shape what research gets done.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They have affected me somewhat to a lot, though I say that as a white woman who has not had the same direct experiences. The protests and conversations pushed me to think harder about what I had noticed growing up but did not name, like who got watched at school or who seemed nervous around police. In the lab and in science more broadly, it also made me think about access: who gets encouraged, who gets assumed competent, and who has to prove themselves over and over.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend protests?
follow_ups.response: No, I did not attend a protest. I mostly read, donated a small amount once, and talked with friends.

follow_ups.question: Was there a conversation that stayed with you?
follow_ups.response: Maya talked about environmental justice and policing in the same breath, and that made me connect issues I had kept separate.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the movement raises real questions about accountability, unequal treatment, and whose pain gets believed. I do not pretend to have every policy answer, but I think data transparency, de-escalation, independent review, and investing in mental health response all make sense. I also think white people like me have to tolerate discomfort without making the conversation about our feelings. My approach has been to listen more, read more carefully, and support changes that are specific rather than symbolic only.

follow_ups.question: What sources shaped your thinking?
follow_ups.response: Long-form journalism, local reporting, books and essays friends recommended, and some policy explainers from universities.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable talking about it?
follow_ups.response: More than I used to, but I am careful. I would rather ask questions than perform certainty.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think about race as something built into systems, not just individual attitudes. Growing up in the Central Valley, I was around a lot of cultural diversity, but my own family background was white, Irish-German, and working class, so I could miss things. Recently I have thought more about how race interacts with education, housing, health, farm labor, air quality, and who gets exposed to risk. I am trying to be less defensive and more observant.

follow_ups.question: How does the Central Valley shape that view?
follow_ups.response: You see labor, immigration, language, class, and environmental exposure all layered together. It makes simple national talking points feel incomplete.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed how you act at work?
follow_ups.response: I try to notice who gets interrupted, who gets credit, and whether interns from less traditional backgrounds are being supported.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and some family, mostly in smaller conversations. I have not joined protests, but I have donated a little, read more, and tried to support equity efforts at work and in science outreach.

follow_ups.question: How do family conversations go?
follow_ups.response: Mixed. My mom listens, my dad gets quiet, and I try to keep it concrete instead of accusatory.

follow_ups.question: What does supporting equity at work mean?
follow_ups.response: Backing structured mentoring, clear expectations, and outreach to local community college students.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends are generally more engaged than my family. Maya talks about race through environmental justice and public health, and Elise is more focused on representation in art spaces. My parents are sympathetic to fairness but get uncomfortable with phrases like systemic racism because they hear it as blame. Evan is younger and more online, so he is quicker to use activist language, sometimes without much patience.

follow_ups.question: Do these differences cause conflict?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes at family dinners, but usually we steer away before it turns ugly.

follow_ups.question: Who challenges you the most?
follow_ups.response: Maya, because she is practical and well-read. She pushes me without making me shut down.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Physically I am mostly healthy. I am active enough with walking, yoga, and hiking, though I sit too much on data-analysis days. I have seasonal allergies and occasional tension headaches, especially when I am stressed or dehydrated. Emotionally, anxiety is the main health issue I manage. It is not constant panic, but it shows up as overthinking, tight shoulders, trouble sleeping, and needing routines to feel steady.

follow_ups.question: Do you take regular medication?
follow_ups.response: No daily prescription right now. I use over-the-counter allergy medicine when needed.

follow_ups.question: How often do headaches happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, more if work is intense or the air quality is bad.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I stick to routines: meal prep, yoga, walks, and enough sleep. It is hard when the Central Valley heat or smoke makes outdoor activity unpleasant, or when work deadlines make me skip movement and eat whatever is fastest. Money also matters. I can manage basics, but therapy, dental work, or unexpected copays make me hesitate.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit slips first?
follow_ups.response: Sleep, then cooking. Once I am tired, I start buying convenience food.

follow_ups.question: What habit helps most?
follow_ups.response: Yoga. It forces me to breathe and notice tension before it turns into a headache.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge like a broken bone or major diagnosis. The most significant thing was finally naming my anxiety more directly with a primary care doctor. I had a period where I was sleeping badly and getting chest tightness before presentations or instrument-heavy weeks. The doctor ruled out heart concerns and talked with me about anxiety management, therapy options, sleep hygiene, and exercise. I have not started regular therapy because of cost and scheduling, but I use journaling, yoga, and routines more intentionally now.

follow_ups.question: When did that doctor visit happen?
follow_ups.response: About a year ago, after a rough month at work with multiple deadlines.

follow_ups.question: Did you receive a formal diagnosis?
follow_ups.response: The doctor described it as anxiety symptoms and possible generalized anxiety, but I have not had a long psychiatric evaluation.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Anxiety can get in the way, especially with presentations or when an experiment fails and I start blaming myself. I still work, but I may lose sleep or spend too much time checking details. I do not have children to care for.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work because of it?
follow_ups.response: Only once for a mental health day when I had barely slept. Usually I push through.

follow_ups.question: What helps during a workday?
follow_ups.response: A written checklist, stepping outside for five minutes, and asking a coworker to sanity-check the instrument setup.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Yes, in smaller but real ways. My dad has blood pressure issues, and my mom has joint pain that flares when she has been standing too much. They are not helpless, but I worry about them getting older and still acting like they should just tough everything out. I help with online portals and reminders because health systems can be confusing. It adds stress because I am trying to be independent, but I also feel responsible.

follow_ups.question: How often do you help with medical logistics?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a month, more if there is an appointment, lab result, or insurance letter.

follow_ups.question: Who else helps them?
follow_ups.response: My brother helps with physical tasks, but paperwork usually comes to me.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have basic health coverage through work, and I am grateful for that, but it still takes effort. Finding an appointment that does not interfere with lab schedules can be hard. I have postponed dental care and therapy because the out-of-pocket cost made me nervous. My parents have had insurance confusion, especially with referrals and portal messages. We usually get care eventually, but it feels like you need administrative stamina.
